CM Energy said the ongoing project reflects its ability to support European offshore contractors with specialist equipment and integrated solutions, with further plans to develop relationships with vessel owners, offshore contractors and suppliers across the region. articles.title: Samudera Shipping sells two tankers for US$14.5 million
articles.summary: Samudera Shipping Line has agreed to sell two Indonesian-flagged oil tankers for a combined US$14.5 million as part of its fleet management strategy. The company’s subsidiary, PT Samudera Shipping Indonesia, signed the sale agreement with an unrelated Indonesian buyer on 22 October 2026. The transaction covers the...
articles.body: Samudera Shipping Line has agreed to sell two Indonesian-flagged oil tankers for a combined US$14.5 million as part of its fleet management strategy. The company’s subsidiary, PT Samudera Shipping Indonesia, signed the sale agreement with an unrelated Indonesian buyer on 22 October 2026. The transaction covers the 2006-built MT Sinar Agra and MT Sinar Busan. The vessels have deadweight capacities of 11,243 tonnes and 11,277 tonnes, respectively. Both tankers are currently operating under time charter agreements. Subject to the existing charterer’s consent, they will be transferred to the buyer with their charters attached. Delivery is expected during the fourth quarter of 2026. Samudera expects US$6 million disposal gain The transaction will be settled in cash, with a 10% deposit and the remaining 90% payable upon vessel delivery. The two tankers had a combined book value of approximately US$8 million at the end of June 2026. An independent valuation placed their combined market value at around US$13.6 million as of 30 September. After estimated transaction costs and before tax, Samudera expects to record a disposal gain of approximately US$6 million. Net proceeds are estimated at US$14 million. Samudera plans to use the funds for general working capital, fleet renewal or other investment opportunities. The company said the sale followed a review of the vessels’ age, condition, employment and prevailing market conditions. Transaction follows earlier tanker disposals The agreement follows Samudera’s disposal of MT Sinar Malahayati and MT Sinar Mendawai earlier in 2026. Those transactions were completed in June and July. When combined with the earlier sales, the latest transaction is classified as a discloseable transaction under Singapore Exchange rules. The sale comes as Samudera continues to reshape its fleet. The company recently signed shipbuilding contracts for two new 3,000 TEU container vessels.

articles.title: DenAr takes on Turkey’s first offshore wind seabed survey campaign
articles.summary: Turkish marine survey specialist DenAr Ocean Engineering Services has been selected by the country’s Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources to carry out geophysical and geotechnical seabed investigations for Turkey’s first offshore wind development programme. articles.body: Europe Offshore Renewables DenAr takes on Turkey’s first offshore wind seabed survey campaign Bojan Lepic November 6, 2026 0 0 1 minute read DeNar DeNar Turkish marine survey specialist DenAr Ocean Engineering Services has been selected by the country’s Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources to carry out geophysical and geotechnical seabed investigations for Turkey’s first offshore wind development programme. The NCS-01 project covers two areas in the Sea of Marmara and forms part of the government initiative to prepare prospective offshore wind sites for future development. The scope includes multibeam bathymetric surveys, side-scan sonar, sub-bottom profiling, magnetometer measurements, ultra-high-resolution seismic investigations and unexploded ordnance surveys. DenAr will also undertake offshore cone penetration testing and seabed sampling using its DP2 survey vessel DenAr Explorer , supported by laboratory testing and geotechnical reporting. The company has identified DenAr , DenAr Explorer , DenAr Surveyor and Salvor among the vessels being mobilised for the programme. The contract forms part of Turkey’s EU-supported Offshore Wind Energy Support Project, implemented with World Bank involvement. The programme also includes wind-resource measurements, feasibility assessments, grid-connection studies and environmental investigations covering prospective offshore wind development areas around Bandırma, Şarköy, and Karabiga. The survey results are intended to reduce development risks and establish the technical basis for future offshore wind tenders. articles.title: Khalid Hashim set to pass the baton at Precious Shipping
articles.summary: Thailand’s Precious Shipping is preparing a change at the top, with longtime managing director Khalid Moinuddin Hashim moving to executive vice chairman and finance chief Gautam Khurana taking over the running of the Bangkok-listed dry bulk owner. The company’s board approved the leadership reshuffle, with both...
articles.body: Asia Dry Cargo Khalid Hashim set to pass the baton at Precious Shipping Adis Ajdin November 6, 2026 0 88 1 minute read Thailand’s Precious Shipping is preparing a change at the top, with longtime managing director Khalid Moinuddin Hashim moving to executive vice chairman and finance chief Gautam Khurana taking over the running of the Bangkok-listed dry bulk owner. The company’s board approved the leadership reshuffle, with both appointments taking effect on January 1, 2027, according to a filing with the Stock Exchange of Thailand. Khurana will continue to serve as director of finance until a successor is appointed. Both executives will retain their seats on the company’s board of directors and executive board. The transition marks a significant shift for Precious Shipping, which has been led by Hashim for more than three decades. He helped build the company into one of Thailand’s most prominent dry bulk owners following its establishment in 1989 and stock market listing in 1993. Khurana joined Precious in 2018 as chief financial officer before becoming finance director in 2019. His earlier career included a decade at DVB Bank in London and Singapore, where he worked in maritime finance, structured asset financing and leasing. The management shake-up comes amid a major fleet renewal programme that has seen Precious sell ageing handysize and supramax vessels while expanding its ultramax fleet. In September, the company returned to China’s Taizhou Sanfu Ship Engineering for four 64,500 dwt ultramax newbuildings worth a combined $141.8m, with deliveries scheduled between April 2030 and January 2031. The order followed an earlier $133.46m contract for four 63,500 dwt ultramaxes at the same yard, with two vessels already in service and the remaining pair due through the first quarter of 2027. Once the outstanding newbuildings arrive, Precious expects its fleet to reach 47 vessels totalling about 2.34m dwt. The owner has also started diversifying beyond dry bulk, entering the MR product tanker market earlier this year through direct acquisitions and its 45%-owned Nusantara Maritime joint venture. articles.title: IMO launches survey on Maritime Single Windows
articles.summary: The IMO has launched a survey with the view to gathering information on the level of implementation and use of Maritime Single Window (MSW) systems to better understand the impact of MSW implementation on the administrative workload of maritime stakeholders and users. articles.body: IMO launches survey on Maritime Single Windows in International Shipping News 06/11/2026 The IMO has launched a survey with the view to gathering information on the level of implementation and use of Maritime Single Window (MSW) systems to better understand the impact of MSW implementation on the administrative workload of maritime stakeholders and users. Maritime Single Windows (MSW) are a means of reducing a ship’s reporting burden by enabling information required for a port call to be exchanged once, digitally and efficiently, using harmonised data standards that allow different authorities and systems to interoperate. However, there is a need to test whether MSWs are actually delivering the benefits they were introduced to achieve. As such, the IMO has launched a survey with the view to gathering information on the level of implementation and use of MSW systems by the end of 2026. It is envisaged that a follow-up survey will be conducted in 2028 to assess developments since 2026 and to better understand the impact of MSW implementation on the administrative workload of maritime stakeholders and users. The survey is open to all interested stakeholders with experience in the implementation, operation or use of MSW systems. In order to ensure the accuracy and relevance of the analysis, certain questions are mandatory, including those relating to the country concerned and the respondent’s organisation type or stakeholder category. The information provided will enable the IMO Secretariat to analyse responses by country and stakeholder group and to identify common trends, challenges and good practices. The survey seeks to collect the views and experiences of all relevant stakeholders involved in the submission, processing and use of information through MSW systems, including public authorities and private-sector users. The information gathered will support the work of the IMO in identifying common challenges, good practices and opportunities to further improve the implementation and operation of MSW systems. BIMCO members are encouraged to submit their responses by 30 November 2026. The Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important shipping routes, has become a dangerous war zone due to the conflict between Iran and the United States, leaving thousands of seafarers stranded and exposing them to missile and mine attacks. According to the International Transport Workers’ Federation, many crews face severe shortages of food, drinking water, fuel, medical assistance, and unpaid wages, while more than 40 sailors have reportedly been killed. The organization criticizes some shipowners for continuing to send vessels into the high-risk area despite the obvious dangers to crews. Shipping companies such as Hapag-Lloyd say they have prioritized crew safety over profits, rerouting ships and accepting significant financial losses to avoid conflict zones. Experts warn that if growing numbers of experienced seafarers refuse to return to sea, global supply chains and international trade could face serious long-term disruptions. articles.summary: India can accelerate the industrial scale-up of its shipbuilding and ship-repair sector by creating a 10-year vessel procurement pipeline that will provide long-term demand visibility, a report by consulting firm EY and industry chamber FICCI said. The report, titled “Optimising India’s Shipbuilding and Ship Repair...
articles.body: India should create 10-year vessel procurement pipeline: EY-FICCI report in International Shipping News 06/11/2026 India can accelerate the industrial scale-up of its shipbuilding and ship-repair sector by creating a 10-year vessel procurement pipeline that will provide long-term demand visibility, a report by consulting firm EY and industry chamber FICCI said. The report, titled “Optimising India’s Shipbuilding and Ship Repair Capacity: Roadmap for Industrial Scale-up”, recommended considering a national maritime demand and market assurance mechanism to consolidate requirements from public sector undertakings (PSUs), ports, coastal shipping operators, inland-waterway agencies and other major vessel users into a structured, rolling 10-year procurement pipeline. “Standard vessel platforms and repeat procurement programmes could further improve shipyard productivity, supplier investment and financing access,” the report said. India delivered ships with a combined gross tonnage (GT) of 57,637 in 2025, representing approximately 0.075 per cent of global output. Although output improved over 2024, the longer-term trend remains uneven, the report said. “Domestic demand can provide the required order visibility. As of December 2025, 1,071 vessels in the Indian fleet were either more than 20 years old or aged 16–20 years. This presents a significant fleet-renewal opportunity, alongside demand from coastal shipping, inland waterways, port services and selected commercial vessel categories,” it added. The report’s recommendations include strengthening maritime financing through long-tenure construction finance, working capital and refund-guarantee support, and deepening domestic supply chains by developing capabilities in critical marine equipment, supported by testing, certification and common vendor-qualification standards. It also calls for scaling shipbuilding and ship repair together to create stronger utilisation of infrastructure, skills and supplier networks, along with developing integrated maritime clusters around major shipbuilding and repair locations to strengthen access to suppliers, logistics, skills and supporting infrastructure. India’s geographic position provides an opportunity to expand its ship-repair capabilities. Approximately 7-9 per cent of global maritime traffic passes within 300 nautical miles of its coastline, while its current share of the global ship-repair market indicates scope for further growth. articles.title: Advancing maritime digitalization in West and Central Africa
articles.summary: The digitalization of ports across nine West and Central African countries has been boosted through a regional workshop in Accra, Ghana. The event was organized by IMO, the Africa Transport Policy Program (SSATP), and the World Bank, in partnership with the Ghana Maritime Authority. The key aims of the event...
articles.body: Advancing maritime digitalization in West and Central Africa in International Shipping News 06/11/2026 The digitalization of ports across nine West and Central African countries has been boosted through a regional workshop in Accra, Ghana. The event was organized by IMO, the Africa Transport Policy Program (SSATP), and the World Bank, in partnership with the Ghana Maritime Authority. The key aims of the event included: • Promoting the adoption of the IMO Compendium on Facilitation and Electronic Business, which sets out how shipping and port data are structured and shared electronically to streamline communication; and • Scaling up the implementation of Maritime Single Windows (MSWs) and Port Community Systems (PCSs), which are integrated digital platforms that streamline vessel and cargo clearance, reduce bureaucratic delays, and will help to strengthen Africa’s competitiveness in global maritime trade. A central principle of the workshop was that MSW systems are not standalone digital solutions but core elements of a broader, regionally harmonized trade facilitation ecosystem. MSW systems are mandatory under IMO’s Facilitation (FAL) Convention. Promoting regional collaboration The workshop convened regional and international institutions committed to translating policy into action, including the Port Management Association of West and Central Africa (PMAWCA), the African Development Bank (AfDB), the African Harbour Masters’ Committee (AHMC), and the African Alliance for Electronic Commerce (AAEC). The workshop was structured around both knowledge sharing and practical capacity building, with 55 participants, including 15 women, from maritime administrations, port authorities, and customs authorities in Cabo Verde, Equatorial Guinea, The Gambia, Ghana, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Nigeria, São Tomé and Príncipe, and Sierra Leone. Sessions highlighted the strategic benefits of MSW implementation and the need to align with the IMO Compendium on Facilitation and Electronic Business, with sharing of lessons and good practices from regional IMO needs assessment missions, including analyses of ship and cargo clearance systems, key challenges, and recommendations for effective MSW deployment. Participating Member States presented their port systems, fostering peer learning on progress, challenges, and opportunities. Supporting a regional trade facilitation ecosystem The workshop explored potential synergies between Port Community Systems and MSWs to further enhance port efficiency and trade facilitation. Deepening participants’ understanding of the FAL Convention, strengthening coordination among port stakeholders, and clarifying the financing and policy requirements for MSW implementation, the workshop helped equip countries with the practical knowledge needed to accelerate MSW deployment. The workshop also drew on the IAPH–World Bank study: “Port Community Systems: Lessons from Global Experience.” Anchoring the Workshop within SSATP’s Strategic Agenda This workshop was the third in a series of regional editions, building on a first workshop, held in Abidjan in December 2025, and a second, delivered in Dar es Salaam in April 2026. This reflects the expanding scale and momentum of the continental effort to advance maritime digitalization. The initiative aligns with SSATP’s Fourth Development Plan (DP4), which prioritizes digitalization of transport and trade corridors across Africa. MSW systems are widely acknowledged as essential for reducing logistics costs, improving efficiency, and strengthening port competitiveness. The workshop was delivered through IMO’s Integrated Technical Cooperation Programme (ITCP) in close collaboration with the World Bank, with resources from the Korea–World Bank Partnership Facility (KWPF) and the Ministry of Transport of Ghana. It built on SSATP’s recent analytical work, “Catching Up on Digital Port Infrastructure for Africa”, which highlights that effective MSW implementation depends not only on digital tools but also on a solid legal framework, strong institutional leadership, and coordinated stakeholder engagement. articles.body: Oldendorff Reflags Two Capesize Vessels to Germany in International Shipping News 06/11/2026 Oldendorff Carriers (Oldendorff) is reflagging two of its Capesize bulk carriers to Germany, underlining the company’s long standing ties to the country and its commitment to Germany’s maritime sector. Earlier today, the Alice Oldendorff officially transferred from the Portuguese to the German flag in Saldanha Bay, South Africa. Capesize bulk carrier Gina Oldendorff is set to follow in the coming months. Both vessels will be registered with Hamburg as their home port. The move has particular significance for Oldendorff. Founded in Hamburg in 1921, the family owned company has grown into one of the world’s largest dry bulk shipping companies, while maintaining close ties to Germany and its maritime community. “Germany has a strong maritime heritage, deep industry expertise and a well-established framework for quality shipping. The improvements to enhance service and support for shipowners, together with the authorities’ commitment to maintaining a consistently high level of service, were important factors in our decision to return these vessels to the German flag. As a German family-owned company, bringing two of our largest bulk carriers under the German flag is a meaningful way for us to reaffirm our roots while supporting the continued strength and competitiveness of Germany’s maritime sector,” says Peter Bagh, Chief Operating Officer at Oldendorff Carriers. The German flag is internationally recognised for its high standards and consistently performs well in international flag state assessments. Its regulatory framework places a strong emphasis on maritime safety, environmental protection and high standards for working and living conditions at sea. “By choosing to bring these vessels under the German flag, Oldendorff is sending a strong signal of confidence in the German flag and Germany as a maritime location,” said Christian Hirte, Parliamentary State Secretary at the Federal Ministry of Transport. “Over the past two years in particular, we have made the German flag considerably more attractive and user-friendly while significantly reducing bureaucracy. I am very pleased that these efforts have convinced Oldendorff Carriers to fly the German flag, and I hope that many more German shipowners will follow their example.” As of September 2026, the German merchant fleet comprises 404 vessels with a combined gross tonnage of approximately 8.86 million GT. With the registration of Alice Oldendorff (181,963 dwt; 93,718 GT) and Gina Oldendorff (182,002 dwt; 93,718 GT), large bulk carriers will return to the German flag for the first time in several years. The two Capesize vessels will be the only large bulk carriers currently operating under the German flag, marking a notable addition to Germany’s merchant fleet. articles.body: Baltic connects with Chinese shipping industry at Shanghai Pudong Shipping Week 2026 in International Shipping News 06/11/2026 Baltic Exchange was once again pleased to take part in Shanghai Pudong International Shipping Week 2026, joining industry leaders from across the maritime sector to strengthen international relationships and discuss the future of global shipping. Held under this year’s theme ‘Steady Shipping, Intelligent Horizons, Shared Ecosystem’, the week explored key industry developments, including digital innovation, supply chain resilience, decarbonisation and sustainability. It also highlighted China’s growing influence in global shipping and Shanghai’s role as an international maritime hub, notably after it ranked second in the 2026 Xinhua-Baltic International Shipping Centre Index. For the Baltic, Shanghai Pudong International Shipping Week 2026 was an opportunity to showcase the importance of the Baltic and its benchmark data to the Chinese shipping community and discuss with like-minded individuals about the importance of collaboration and transparency in driving the global maritime industry forward. One of the highlights of the week was the 2026 Global Maritime Forum Annual Summit, which the Baltic was pleased to once again be a leading sponsor for. The event also included the official networking dinner, where Baltic CEO Mark Jackson spoke to the hundreds of attendees about the importance of the GMF and its role in helping to push the global shipping community forward on key initiatives and policies. Baltic Head of Membership Jos Standerwick was also present at the summit, which brought together industry leaders to discuss shipping’s energy transition, the IMO’s Net-Zero Framework and the wider challenges facing global trade. Reflecting on the GMF summit, Mark Jackson said: “This year’s Global Maritime Forum summit in Shanghai was a vital opportunity for the international shipping community to better understand the complexities of modern trade. As volatility and uncertainty for global shipping markets continue, it was important for our industry to come together to share insights and experiences, and for Baltic Exchange to showcase its role in providing independent market benchmarks to help the market make more informed decisions.” Baltic Exchange also participated in the official UK Day, hosted by the UK Shipping Concierge at the Shanghai International Convention Centre under the theme “UK and China: Navigating Together Towards Safer, Greener Shipping”. Jin Yu Cheong, Head of Baltic Asia, was part of an insightful panel that explored how geopolitics are reshaping global trade and shipping, alongside experts from across the industry. The discussion examined how geopolitical tensions, regulatory changes, cyber threats and climate risks are increasingly interconnected, and how the industry can build resilience in an ever uncertain environment, and included speakers from UK P&I Club, DWF Law, Lloyd’s List Intelligence and the International Group of P&I Clubs. The week provided a valuable opportunity for Baltic Exchange to engage with the Chinese shipping community and engage with partners on the issues shaping the industry. Shanghai Pudong International Shipping Week has become a key event on the maritime calendar, and the Baltic looks forward to returning in 2027. articles.body: GlobalBQS launches One Standard For Every Bunker And On-/Off-Hire Survey in International Shipping News 06/11/2026 GlobalBQS went live on 2 November 2026 with a platform that brings one standard to bunker quantity surveys and on-/off-hire surveys, wherever a vessel is. Today every surveyor reports in their own format. Figures are locked in PDFs, invoices arrive from every port, and when a dispute comes up, owners and charterers end up searching through e-mails. GlobalBQS changes that without changing who does the survey. The client keeps its own surveyor – VPS, Saybolt, FOBAS or any independent surveyor – who reports in the GlobalBQS survey app, on board, online or offline. The surveyor approves a draft, and the final report arrives in the client’s portal and inbox in one standard format, typically within hours. Every survey then becomes data. In the client portal, owners and charterers see where logbook figures and measured ROB drift apart per vessel and grade, which suppliers and barges deliver short, and every letter of protest on record. A fuel chain follows every tonne per charter, from delivery to redelivery. Vessels, suppliers and surveyors are rated on measured facts, against an anonymised network benchmark. “After 18 years at sea and many more in chartering and operations, I have seen too many bunker disputes decided by whoever had the clearest paperwork,” says Capt. Richard van Renswoude, founder of GlobalBQS. “GlobalBQS gives everyone the same standard and the same facts – and every survey makes the picture sharper.” There is no subscription. Clients order by copying [email protected] on their bunker confirmation or in one click in the portal, with one invoice per survey or per month. Surveyor access opens in January 2027. In 2027 the company will also launch Voyager, a service in which GlobalBQS handles the full survey procurement and selects the best surveyor for each job, based on the data. articles.body: Subsea7 Strikes Deal to Sell Seaway7 Heavy Transport Unit to HEA Energy Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 6, 2026 (Credit: Seaway7) Subsea7 has agreed to sell its Seaway7 heavy transportation business, comprising six semi-submersible vessels, to HEA Energy in a transaction linked to its proposed merger with Saipem. The sale covers six open-deck semi-submersible heavy transportation vessels, five of which are owned and one chartered from a third party. According to the Seaway7’s fleet information, the six heavy transportation vessels include Seaway Albatross Seaway Eagle, Seaway Falcon, Seaway Hawk, Seaway Osprey, and Seaway Swan. The transaction remains subject to closing conditions, including applicable regulatory approvals, with completion expected in the first half of 2027. Subsea7 said the commercial terms of the agreement, including the cash consideration, would remain confidential. The divestment constitutes the permitted business sale referenced in Subsea7's merger agreement with Saipem and will trigger a special dividend of $ €105 million, previously approved at an extraordinary general meeting on September 25, 2025. The dividend will be paid at the earlier of the transaction's completion or the date immediately preceding the effective date of the proposed merger with Saipem. Subsea7 said processing and distributing the dividend funds could take up to two weeks.

articles.body: News November 6, 2026 · 10 minutes ago Turkish marine survey specialist secures work on country’s first offshore wind site investigation program AB Adrijana Buljan Offshore Wind 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email DenAr Ocean Engineering Services DenAr Ocean Engineering Services has been awarded a contract by Türkiye’s Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources (MENR) to carry out geophysical and geotechnical ground investigations for the country’s first offshore wind site investigation program. The work covers two areas in the Sea of Marmara designated under the NCS-01 project. The survey scope includes multibeam echosounder (MBES), side-scan sonar, sub-bottom profiler and magnetometer surveys, as well as unexploded ordnance (UXO) investigations and ultra-high-resolution seismic surveys. Geotechnical work will involve seabed cone penetration testing (CPT) and sampling from DenAr’s DP2 vessel Denar Explorer, followed by laboratory testing and reporting. The company said the overall field program will involve three vessels and operations during the winter season. As part of preparations, DenAr held a hazard and operability (HAZOP) meeting aboard Denar Explorer with representatives from MENR, its consultant IMDC and the company’s offshore team. The meeting reviewed the planned survey and geotechnical activities, vessel operations and the requirements for working in the busy waters of the Sea of Marmara. DenAr Ocean Engineering Services The award comes as Türkiye advances preparations for its first offshore wind tender and has set a target of installing 5 GW of offshore wind capacity by 2035. In 2023, MENR launched a tender for site investigation and consultancy services covering three potential development zones in the Sea of Marmara, as part of work on site preparation and the design of the country’s first offshore wind auction. The government published draft rules for a 1 GW offshore wind tender in June 2026 and said in August that it planned to hold the first auction in the first quarter of 2027 . articles.body: Africa Europe Offshore EnerMech picks up Chevron pipeline work off Equatorial Guinea Bojan Lepic November 6, 2026 0 101 1 minute read EnerMech EnerMech UK-headquartered oilfield services specialist EnerMech has secured a contract from Chevron for pipeline pre-commissioning services on the Aseng gas development offshore Equatorial Guinea. The contract covers preparation of approximately 19 km of rigid production flowline connecting the Aseng field to existing offshore infrastructure. EnerMech will provide pre-operational engineering, project management, and specialist pipeline pre-commissioning services, with the project managed from its Houston base. The award is part of Chevron’s wider Aseng Gas Monetization Project, which involves a single-well subsea tieback connecting the Aseng field to the existing Alen platform in water depths of around 800 m. Chevron made a final investment decision on the development earlier this year, and the project is expected to help sustain Equatorial Guinea’s LNG exports into the mid-2030s. Subsea 7 secured a separate installation contract worth between $150m and $300m in April. Its scope covers the transport and installation of the 19 km rigid production flowline, approximately 20 km of umbilicals, subsea structures, and associated tie-ins. EnerMech’s latest contract covers the specialist work required to prepare the pipeline infrastructure for operation. The Aseng development is part of Chevron’s broader efforts to commercialise offshore gas resources in Equatorial Guinea, including potential future developments around the Alen and cross-border Yoyo-Yolanda fields. articles.title: Alfa Laval makes $700m NAVTOR bet
articles.summary: Swedish industrial group Alfa Laval has struck a $700m all-cash deal to acquire Norwegian maritime software specialist NAVTOR, significantly expanding a digital shipping portfolio that already includes StormGeo and Portchain. The Stockholm-listed group has entered into a definitive agreement to buy NAVTOR for...
articles.body: Europe Tech Alfa Laval makes $700m NAVTOR bet Adis Ajdin November 6, 2026 0 144 2 minutes read Alfa Laval Alfa Laval Swedish industrial group Alfa Laval has struck a $700m all-cash deal to acquire Norwegian maritime software specialist NAVTOR, significantly expanding a digital shipping portfolio that already includes StormGeo and Portchain. The Stockholm-listed group has entered into a definitive agreement to buy NAVTOR for SEK6.85bn ($700m), with completion expected during the first quarter of 2027 subject to regulatory approvals. Alfa Laval described the purchase as one of the most significant transactions in its history. NAVTOR will join its Ocean Division, with its platform set to be brought together with StormGeo and Portchain to create a broader digital fleet offering spanning navigation, vessel performance, voyage optimisation and port operations. NAVTOR, founded in Egersund in 2011, employs around 400 people across 13 offices and serves customers in more than 90 countries. Alfa Laval said it expects the business to generate about $194m in revenue this year. “With this acquisition, Alfa Laval will expand its digital offering at a time when real-time decision-making is increasingly complex,” said chief executive Tom Erixon. NAVTOR has grown from an electronic navigation specialist into a wider ship-to-shore software business covering voyage planning, fleet monitoring, vessel performance, digital logbooks and onboard data workflows. Its expansion has also been driven by acquisitions. US technology investor Accel-KKR took a majority stake in NAVTOR in 2020, followed by purchases of performance analytics specialist Tres Solutions in 2021 and digital logbook developer Ingenium Marine in 2022. NAVTOR then combined with Voyager Worldwide in 2023, creating a business whose technology at the time served about 18,000 vessels. Alfa Laval has been assembling its own maritime software stack since buying weather routing and voyage optimisation company StormGeo for NOK3.63bn in 2021. That buildout accelerated again last week when StormGeo acquired Copenhagen-based Portchain, whose network links shipping lines with more than 200 container terminals accounting for over 40% of global container terminal capacity. The technology is being combined with StormGeo’s voyage optimisation tools so vessel speed and arrival decisions can respond to changing berth availability. NAVTOR brings another major layer to that strategy. SplashTech reported only last week that the company had added near-live AIS streaming to NavFleet, while earlier this year it expanded its digital logbook and compliance tools. Alfa Laval also disclosed that a recent NAVTOR internal review identified unspecified compliance matters, prompting the Norwegian company to strengthen its internal controls and compliance programme. The buyer said arrangements have been made to protect it against pre-acquisition liabilities connected with those matters. Erixon said Alfa Laval was confident the issues would be resolved. The acquisition will be funded through a mixture of Alfa Laval’s cash and existing financing programmes and is expected to be neutral to group margins in the short term. articles.title: Indian ship recycling breakthrough hits Brussels roadblock
articles.summary: A European Parliament committee has voted against allowing two Indian shipbreaking yards onto the EU’s approved recycling list, dealing a setback to shipowners pushing for greater access to South Asian dismantling capacity. The Parliament’s environment committee backed an objection this week to the European...
articles.body: Asia Europe Operations Regulatory Indian ship recycling breakthrough hits Brussels roadblock Adis Ajdin November 6, 2026 0 332 2 minutes read Leela Ship Recycling Leela Ship Recycling A European Parliament committee has voted against allowing two Indian shipbreaking yards onto the EU’s approved recycling list, dealing a setback to shipowners pushing for greater access to South Asian dismantling capacity. The Parliament’s environment committee backed an objection this week to the European Commission’s proposal to approve Shree Ram Vessel Scrap and YSI Recyclers, both located in the Alang-Sosiya shipbreaking hub in Gujarat. The two facilities had received preliminary backing from the Commission following inspections intended to establish whether they met the requirements of the EU Ship Recycling Regulation. Their inclusion would make them the first facilities on the Indian subcontinent to join the European list. MEPs opposing the proposal questioned whether yards using the beaching method, in which ships are dismantled on tidal shorelines, could adequately control pollution and hazardous waste. The objection also raised concerns about downstream waste handling, including scrap steel sent to local re-rolling mills that have not been assessed against EU industrial emissions standards. Environmental monitoring cited by campaigners showed elevated levels of toxic substances, including copper, chromium, cadmium and mercury, in the Alang-Sosiya area. “Today’s vote in the European Parliament sends a strong political message to the European Commission,” said Ingvild Jenssen, executive director of NGO Shipbreaking Platform, arguing that approving the facilities despite shortcomings identified during inspections would undermine the regulation’s environmental objectives. The vote puts lawmakers at odds with European shipping interests. Industry association ECSA had urged MEPs to support the Commission’s proposal, arguing that both yards had undergone extensive inspections and had been found compliant with EU standards. ECSA secretary general Sotiris Raptis warned that denying approval to facilities that had passed the assessment process would undermine the credibility of the regulation. Environmental organisations and recycling industry representatives have taken the opposite position, arguing that beaching operations cannot provide sufficient containment of hazardous materials and should not qualify for EU recognition. Campaigners have also challenged the industry’s argument that additional capacity is needed, pointing to more than 2m light displacement tonnes of combined annual capacity at facilities already on the EU list, which they claim is sufficient to handle recent recycling volumes involving EU-flagged and EU-owned ships. Under EU rules, EU-flagged commercial ships subject to the Ship Recycling Regulation must be dismantled at facilities on the approved European list. Opening that list to Indian yards would give owners more recycling options and potentially alter competition with existing approved facilities in Europe and Turkey. The committee vote is not a final rejection. The objection is expected to go before the full European Parliament later in November and does not automatically require the Commission to withdraw its proposal. Member states will also have a say in the approval process. Lloyd’s Register, which awarded approval in principle to Petrobras for the conceptual design of its proposed REVIT I TUPI FPSO unit, describes the AiP as a significant step in the operator’s strategy of leveraging proven offshore production assets to support future field development in Brazil. The concept builds on the detailed design of the FPSO P-68, which is currently operating in the Santos Basin. With project costs, delivery schedules, and execution risk under continued scrutiny, the classification society emphasizes that adaptation of existing FPSO designs is emerging as a practical route to bringing new offshore production capacity online while maintaining confidence in safety and performance. " Across the offshore industry, we're seeing growing interest in how proven FPSO designs can be adapted and redeployed to support new developments. Operators are looking for ways to shorten project timelines, reduce complexity and build on existing operational experience. The REVIT I TUPI project is a strong example of that approach in action, and our assessment provides independent confidence in the concept as it moves forward. The concept incorporates a comprehensive suite of process engineering documentation, including process flow diagrams, piping and instrumentation diagrams, equipment specifications, and supporting technical studies. LR's review also examined the methodology for managing design modifications, ensuring that changes from the original FPSO P-68 configuration can be identified, assessed, and implemented throughout the project lifecycle. articles.title: Shipbuilding boom heads for 2028 delivery crunch
articles.summary: The global shipbuilding orderbook has expanded three and a half times since 2020, while yard capacity has grown by just 30%, setting the stage for an extraordinary delivery squeeze over the next two years. The latest Shipping Market Review from Danish Ship Finance reveals that shipbuilding order cover has jumped from...
articles.body: Shipyards Shipbuilding boom heads for 2028 delivery crunch Sam Chambers November 6, 2026 0 1,346 2 minutes read Hengli Heavy Industries Hengli Heavy Industries The global shipbuilding orderbook has expanded three and a half times since 2020, while yard capacity has grown by just 30%, setting the stage for an extraordinary delivery squeeze over the next two years. The latest Shipping Market Review from Danish Ship Finance reveals that shipbuilding order cover has jumped from 1.4 years in 2020 to 3.7 years today, with the orderbook now equivalent to 19% of the existing world fleet, up from just 7% six years ago. The figures add another dimension to the remarkable shipbuilding boom documented by Splash on Monday, when Clarksons Research revealed that the global orderbook had reached a record 226.1m compensated gross tonnes (cgt), surpassing the previous peak of 225.5m cgt set in September 2008. Worth approximately $700bn, the backlog is heavily concentrated in China, whose yards control 68% of outstanding orders. Danish Ship Finance notes that shipyards have contracted more tonnage than they have delivered every year since 2021, despite output from active yards increasing 69% over the period. Production is now running at 86% of capacity. The problem is that the delivery pipeline is becoming increasingly unrealistic. The highest-performing yards are booked at 164% of their available capacity for 2028, making substantial delays almost inevitable. Danish Ship Finance’s analysis of five years of individual vessel schedules shows that approximately 78% of contracted tonnage arrives in its scheduled year. Roughly one-sixth slips into subsequent years, while around 5% is cancelled. Even allowing for historical delivery performance, scheduled production in 2027 and 2028 would occupy between 84% and 89% of global yard capacity before delayed vessels from previous years are considered. The Danish financier estimates that 10m to 11m cgt of scheduled deliveries could slip annually from 2027 and 2028. If delayed 2027 deliveries roll into 2028, the latter year’s workload could climb to around 60m cgt, equivalent to 107% of available capacity. The implications extend well beyond shipyard scheduling. Danish Ship Finance warns that in the VLCC, suezmax, capesize and large gas carrier segments, even scrapping every vessel older than 20 years would not offset the incoming orderbook. That raises the prospect of significant pressure on older vessel values as new tonnage arrives. Meanwhile, Clarksons is tracking approximately 225 shipyard expansion projects worldwide, more than three-quarters of them in China. The ballooning shipyard capacity scene in Asia garnered much discussion at the Splash-organised Maritime CEO Forum in Monaco last week. “We have been seeing a lot of new yards popping up, left, right, and centre, and the zombie shipyards being revived,” Milena Pappas from Star Bulk told delegates attending the exclusive shipowner gathering. On concerns about the capabilities of some new yards, Pappas revealed that prospective builders had asked owners to arrange the supply of engines themselves. Cesare d’Amico, who heads up Italian shipowner d’Amico Società di Navigazione warned on the potential for overcapacity. “The number of ships that can be added every day, every week is really a lot,” he said, a point of view shared by John Michael Radziwill, the chairman of Monaco owner CTM. “It will get oversupplied. You’re not going to have a shortage of dry cargo ships for very long,” Radziwill said. articles.body: Middle East Operations Tankers Seafarer missing in Gulf tanker strike as Iran redraws Hormuz blacklist Adis Ajdin November 6, 2026 0 568 3 minutes read U.S. Central Command U.S. Central Command A seafarer is missing following a missile-suspected attack on a Greek-operated tanker deep inside the Arabian Gulf, while Iran has reshuffled its growing Strait of Hormuz blacklist and fresh security warnings point to continuing threats to commercial shipping. The Marshall Islands-flagged Velos Sapphire , a 74,998 dwt product tanker built in 2007 and managed by Athens-based Velos Tankers, was struck around 50 nautical miles north of Qatar’s Madinat ash Shamal. UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) initially reported two unidentified projectiles hitting an unnamed tanker at 23:20 UTC. The ship’s operator subsequently reported an explosion on the aft port side, believed to have been caused by an unidentified missile. The International Maritime Organization (IMO) has since identified the vessel, recording damage, no pollution and one seafarer missing. Maritime security sources have reported that the crew member was killed, although the IMO has not confirmed a fatality.A fire reportedly broke out following the strike but was extinguished. The tanker had departed Fujairah on November 3 bound for Sitra, Bahrain. AIS analysis showed its speed falling to 2.4 knots shortly before the attack and to around 1.1 knots afterwards. It subsequently regained speed and continued towards Bahrain, suggesting it retained propulsion despite the damage. The strike adds to growing concerns that attacks on merchant shipping are spreading well beyond the Hormuz chokepoint. The vessel does not appear on Iran’s blacklist of ships accused of breaching its transit requirements. Another tanker in the same Greek-managed fleet, Velos Amber, is listed, although there is no established connection between the blacklist and the latest attack. Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) has meanwhile removed two LPG carriers sanctioned by Washington from its non-compliance list. The 2003-built Gas Marakua and 2001-built SOGL , both designated by the US Treasury in October over their links to Iranian petroleum shipping networks, disappeared from the latest list published on November 5. The authority has instead added the 2018-built, Panama-flagged chemical and products tanker Mercan , which is owned and operated from Turkey. The changes leave 239 vessels on Tehran’s blacklist, down from 240 earlier in the week but sharply higher than the 77 recorded in September. PGSA has provided no explanation for the changes. The authority has threatened blacklisted vessels with fines, detention or confiscation during future passages, while also warning that ships cooperating with designated vessels through ship-to-ship transfers could face restrictions. The overlapping sanctions regimes have created further difficulties for operators. Washington has designated PGSA itself and warned that obtaining services or safe-passage guarantees from the Iranian authority can expose shipping companies to sanctions risks. Mine threats have also returned to the forefront. The US has called on Iran to identify mine locations in the Strait of Hormuz during discussions at the IMO, while Iranian forces have separately claimed several tanker mine strikes without identifying the vessels involved. Tehran has claimed incidents involving five tankers and a tugboat, including fires and mine damage, but the reports remain independently unverified. It is also unclear whether some of the claims overlap with previously reported attacks. A maritime security assessment issued on Thursday by the Joint Maritime Information Centre (JMIC) recorded four attacks in the strait during its latest 96-hour reporting period, all concentrated within 52 hours off Oman’s Musandam peninsula between November 1 and 3. Two further attacks were recorded inside the Arabian Gulf. JMIC continues to classify the threat around Hormuz as severe, warning of further deliberate strikes and highlighting drone overflights, targeted surveillance and radio harassment of merchant vessels. Shipping traffic remains severely depressed. AIS-based monitoring recorded just nine commercial crossings on Thursday, with the seven-day average running at around nine ships a day, barely a tenth of the pre-conflict level of approximately 85. South Korea is also preparing to expand its Cheonghae naval unit’s operational area towards southern Oman and reinforce it with a P-8A maritime patrol aircraft and mine-countermeasure capabilities. The proposal, which requires parliamentary approval, would not place the unit inside Hormuz but could support future mine-clearance operations. Diplomatic efforts continue in parallel, with the foreign ministers of Oman and Iran discussing practical and technical arrangements for restoring unhindered navigation through the strait on Thursday. No reopening agreement has been announced. The IMO’s latest figures put the number of confirmed maritime incidents across the region at 129, with 24 seafarer fatalities recorded since the conflict began. articles.body: Contributions Operations Shipping has a coffee problem Splash November 6, 2026 0 515 2 minutes read From Posidonia to Geneva Dry, the shipping industry’s favourite pastime appears to be arranging coffee meetings that may or may not actually happen. Mike Darby from Merchant Recruitment makes the case for the Baltic Flat White Index. In bunkering, the cappuccino effect means paying for froth instead of fuel. At shipping conferences, it’s practically the business model. All this talk about alternative fuels for ships but has anyone stopped to consider what actually fuels the people running them? LNG, methanol, ammonia, hydrogen. Billions being invested in finding the fuel of the future, while the maritime industry continues to operate almost entirely on caffeine and vaguely agreed diary appointments. I’m increasingly convinced that approximately 70% of the shipping industry is trying to arrange a coffee with the other 30%. “Let’s grab a coffee at Posidonia.” “Are you around for a quick coffee at Geneva Dry?” “We should definitely catch up in Hamburg.” “Next time you’re in London, let’s get something in the diary.” At this point, I’m surprised coffee beans haven’t become a recognised dry bulk commodity benchmark, with their own Baltic index and a dedicated team of brokers fixing shipments between Brazil and whichever city happens to be hosting the next major maritime conference. I’m fairly certain Geneva Dry alone is responsible for at least one additional vessel being chartered to transport coffee beans into Europe each year. A fully laden supramax, diverted from its original voyage to ensure several thousand shipping professionals can spend three days arranging meetings they could probably have had on Teams. You can imagine the freight market reacting accordingly: “Brazil–Geneva coffee bean rates firming ahead of conference season. Strong demand from charterers, limited prompt tonnage and reports of several brokers already on their sixth flat white before 10am.” There’s a particular art to the conference coffee meeting. You agree to meet at 10am. At 9:55, one person messages to say they’re running ten minutes late. At 10:12, the other realises they’re waiting at the wrong entrance. By 10:25, you’ve finally found each other, only to discover there’s nowhere to sit. So you end up standing next to a bin, holding a coffee that’s approximately the temperature of the sun, discussing the dry bulk market while simultaneously trying not to spill it down somebody’s very expensive suit. Then there’s the person who manages to arrange eight coffee meetings between 9am and midday. An impressive achievement considering each meeting is apparently going to last 30 minutes, nobody knows where they’re meeting and the exhibition centre is roughly the size of a small European country. Of course, not every coffee meeting actually involves coffee. By lunchtime, somebody inevitably suggests switching to something stronger. By 4pm, the original coffee meeting has somehow turned into drinks, dinner and a discussion about whether anyone actually knows who’s paying. Then there’s the classic closing line: ”We must do this more often.” Which, translated into shipping language, means we’ll probably bump into each other in Athens next June, promise to arrange another coffee and repeat the entire process. For an industry responsible for coordinating the movement of billions of tonnes of cargo around the world, we’re remarkably bad at coordinating two people and a cappuccino, but perhaps that’s part of the charm. Shipping remains a relationship-driven industry, and despite all the technology, digitalisation and virtual meetings, there’s still something valuable about sitting down with someone face-to-face. Even if it takes 40 minutes to find them. So while the industry continues debating the merits of LNG, methanol and ammonia, I think we’ve overlooked the most important fuel of all. Coffee. If everyone who promised to “grab one soon” actually followed through, we’d probably need to charter another capesize. articles.title: AskChief expands maritime AI platform after surpassing 100 vessels
articles.summary: Maritime artificial intelligence company AskChief has opened its specialised AI platform to the wider shipping market after surpassing 100 vessels in less than a year of live use with shipowners and ship managers. The company, which has offices in Athens and London, said its technology is already being used by...
articles.body: Maritime artificial intelligence company AskChief has opened its specialised AI platform to the wider shipping market after surpassing 100 vessels in less than a year of live use with shipowners and ship managers. The company, which has offices in Athens and London, said its technology is already being used by maritime operators including Seanergy Maritime, Castor Ships, Iblea, Delia and IMECS, part of the ITOCHU Group. According to AskChief, customer usage of its platform typically triples within the first 90 days of deployment, indicating growing adoption among technical and compliance teams. The expansion marks a new stage in the company’s commercial development, following initial deployments that helped shape its two specialised solutions, AskChief Technical and AskChief Compliance. AI applications for technical and compliance operations AskChief’s platform is designed to help shipping companies access and use operational knowledge stored across technical manuals, safety management systems (SMS), vessel records and previous incidents. AskChief Technical supports troubleshooting and technical operations by bringing together relevant documentation and historical fleet experience. AskChief Compliance focuses on regulatory procedures, compliance checks, audit preparation and the identification of supporting evidence. Both solutions use information drawn from each operator’s own documentation and operational history, allowing technical and HSQE teams to retrieve relevant material without manually searching through multiple sources. The platform can also support multi-step tasks by gathering and examining information before preparing it for professional review. According to the company, the system provides visibility into its sources while leaving operational decisions and professional judgement with the relevant personnel. “AskChief AI turns advanced technical and compliance expertise into clear answers for our shipping professionals to use in real time, onboard our vessels and at the office. That’s the kind of tool a modern fleet should be running,” said Stamatis Tsantanis, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Seanergy Maritime Holdings Corp. AskChief targets wider maritime adoption The company said its development has been informed by feedback from technical and HSQE professionals working both onboard vessels and in shore-based offices. “Generic AI can give you an answer. Specialised AI moves the work forward,” said Michalis Gkontas, Co-Founder and CEO of AskChief. “AskChief is built around each shipping company’s own knowledge and experience. After proving this approach in live maritime operations, we are ready to bring it to the wider market.” Vassilis Mavrogiannis, Co-Founder and Chief Maritime Officer at AskChief, highlighted the challenge of accessing relevant operational information when technical decisions need to be made. “After 20 years in maritime, including as a technical manager, I learned that expertise is rarely the bottleneck. The bottleneck is getting the right evidence in front of the right person at the right time,” said Mavrogiannis. He added that the platform is intended to support superintendents, chief engineers and designated persons ashore (DPAs) by assembling information from technical manuals, vessel histories and previous cases, allowing them to concentrate on evaluating evidence and making decisions. With its platform now available to shipowners and ship managers across the wider market, AskChief is seeking to extend the use of specialised AI in technical management, regulatory compliance and fleet knowledge management.

articles.summary: Australia has completed its first green ammonia bunkering operation involving an ammonia-powered bulk carrier, marking another step toward bringing alternative fuels into commercial shipping. The operation took place earlier this...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network The ammonia-powered bulk carrier Mineral Europa receives green ammonia during a ship-to-ship bunkering operation at the Port of Port Hedland, Australia. Photo: Fortescue Australia has completed its first green ammonia bunkering operation involving an ammonia-powered bulk carrier, marking another step toward bringing alternative fuels into commercial shipping. The operation took place earlier this week at the Port of Port Hedland in Western Australia, where the 300-meter Mineral Europa received certified green ammonia from a bunker vessel before entering port to load iron ore bound for China. The vessel, described as the world’s first ammonia-powered dry bulk carrier, is operated by CMB.TECH and chartered to Australian mining giant Fortescue. According to a joint announcement from Fortescue, Pilbara Ports and CMB.TECH , the ship-to-ship transfer took approximately two hours and was completed successfully at 8:42 a.m. local time. The operation required extensive planning, including vessel compatibility assessments, ammonia dispersion modeling, emergency response procedures, and additional marine support. Port authorities said the trial proceeded only after all safety and operational requirements had been met. The successful bunkering is particularly significant for the iron ore trade, which relies heavily on large bulk carriers transporting Australian exports to Asian steelmakers. Fortescue is seeking to reduce emissions from those voyages by introducing ammonia-powered vessels and developing a reliable supply of green marine fuel. Unlike conventional marine fuels, ammonia contains no carbon and produces no carbon dioxide when used as fuel. Its overall emissions benefits, however, depend on how it is produced and on controlling other emissions, including nitrous oxide. Ammonia’s toxicity also presents additional challenges for ship operators, ports and bunker suppliers. Fortescue Metals CEO Dino Otranto said the operation demonstrated that ammonia bunkering is moving beyond small-scale testing toward practical use in major commercial ports. “Industry has moved ahead of regulation to prove the technology,” Otranto said. He added that policy certainty and long-term fuel purchasing commitments would be needed to support further investment in green ammonia production and bunkering infrastructure. Fortescue has been an early supporter of ammonia as a marine fuel. In 2024, its Fortescue Green Pioneer completed ammonia-fueled propulsion trials in Singapore , demonstrating the technology aboard a converted offshore support vessel. The company has since expanded its commercial shipping ambitions through a partnership with CMB.TECH. In addition to Mineral Europa , Fortescue charters nine other vessels from the shipping group that can be converted to operate on ammonia in the future. The companies also announced an agreement earlier this year covering up to 12 ammonia-capable bulk carriers. The Port Hedland operation builds on an earlier ship-to-ship ammonia transfer trial at nearby Dampier in September 2024 , which helped establish procedures for handling ammonia between vessels. Pilbara Ports is now studying the development of a clean fuel bunkering hub in the region, with the latest trial expected to inform future operations. While ammonia-powered shipping still faces substantial hurdles involving fuel cost, availability, safety and regulatory standards, the Port Hedland operation demonstrates how the fuel could be supplied to large commercial vessels at one of the world’s busiest bulk export ports. The companies did not disclose the quantity of green ammonia transferred during the operation. articles.summary: A Finnish court on Thursday jailed the Russian captain and an Azerbaijani crew member of the cargo ship Fitburg for aggravated sabotage over damage to two subsea telecommunications cables in the Gulf of Finland last year.

Finnish Police/Handout via REUTERS HELSINKI, Nov 5 (Reuters) – A Finnish court on Thursday jailed the Russian captain and an Azerbaijani crew member of the cargo ship Fitburg for aggravated sabotage over damage to two subsea telecommunications cables in the Gulf of Finland last year. Finland on December 31 seized the vessel in the Gulf of Finland while it was en route from Russia to Israel, on suspicion that it had damaged cables running from Helsinki to Estonia. The Helsinki District Court sentenced the captain to 3 years and 6 months in prison and the crew member to 2 years and 10 months. It said in a statement the two acted intentionally when the ship dragged an anchor chain and anchor shank along the seabed for around 130 km (81 miles). Finland has intensified efforts to protect its undersea infrastructure following a string of incidents affecting cables and pipelines in the Baltic Sea since 2022, including a vessel-boarding drill it conducted in September. The captain will appeal the verdict, while the crew member has not yet decided whether to do so, their respective lawyers said. The court also ordered the two defendants to jointly pay around €1.9 million ($2.1 million) in damages, and ordered the captain to pay about €85,000 more, the verdict showed. The seized vessel, sailing under Saint Vincent and the Grenadines’ flag, was en route from the Russian port of St Petersburg to Israel at the time of the incident. The ship has since been released. The defendants, who have remained in Finland subject to travel bans, have denied any wrongdoing and have challenged Finland’s jurisdiction in the case. The 14 crew members of the vessel were nationals of Russia, Georgia, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan, investigators have said. articles.title: Arc Begins Battery-Electric Conversion of Long Beach Harbor Tug
articles.summary: Arc, a marine technology company, has begun engineering the battery-electric conversion of Harbor Sentinel, a 50-foot harbor tug owned and operated by Pacific Maritime Group (PMG). Supported by funding from the Port of Long Beach through its Technology Advancement Program (TAP) and SWIFT Program…
articles.body: Arc Begins Battery-Electric Conversion of Long Beach Harbor Tug Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 5, 2026 © PMG Arc, a marine technology company, has begun engineering the battery-electric conversion of Harbor Sentinel, a 50-foot harbor tug owned and operated by Pacific Maritime Group (PMG). Supported by funding from the Port of Long Beach through its Technology Advancement Program (TAP) and SWIFT Program, along with a Volkswagen Environmental Mitigation Trust grant administered by the Bay Area Air Quality Management District, the project will replace the tug’s twin diesel engines with an Arc electric powertrain. Naval architecture firm Glosten is leading vessel engineering. Following commissioning, Harbor Sentinel will return to work from PMG’s Long Beach terminal for a 12-month demonstration. The Harbor Sentinel joined PMG’s harbor fleet in 2023. The tug currently runs on two Cummins KT19 diesel engines producing 950 horsepower and carries 8,900 gallons of fuel. Its work includes moving barges and supporting construction and shipyard operations. In converting to electric power, the tug joins other efforts by the California Air Resources Board (CARB) to improve the air quality in California. Glosten completed a feasibility study and hull scan before engineering began. The firm is now adapting the vessel and designing onboard systems to meet applicable U.S. Coast Guard Subchapter M requirements. PMG will remove both diesel engines and install an integrated electric powertrain tailored to the existing vessel. The system includes a battery bank targeting 2 MWh of usable energy, electric motors and drivetrain, power electronics for the vessel’s existing AC equipment, updated helm controls and captain displays, and onboard charging with a DC fast-charge inlet. Telematics will support 24/7 remote monitoring. To accommodate the system, PMG in-house will widen the Sentinel 3.5’ and build a new deck, midbody, and pilothouse. Arc will integrate, commission and test the system, then support PMG’s crew on site and remotely after the tug returns to service. Arc will also prepare the technical documentation required for Coast Guard review of its systems and components. The Port of Long Beach’s Technology Advancement Program supports demonstrations of emerging technologies on working port equipment as part of the San Pedro Bay Ports Clean Air Action Plan. During the 12-month demonstration, Arc will collect data on performance, operations and charging, report results to the Port quarterly, and deliver a final report evaluating the technology and its potential for broader commercial adoption. This project compliments other conversion projects in the Port of Los Angeles. Through the Harbor Sentinel conversion, Arc and Pacific Maritime Group aim to demonstrate the technical and economic feasibility of repowering existing commercial vessels with electric propulsion systems.

articles.summary: The Trump administration has approved a $1 billion offshore crude oil export project off the coast of Louisiana, clearing a major regulatory hurdle for a facility designed to load some...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Shutterstock/Sven Hansche The Trump administration has approved a $1 billion offshore crude oil export project off the coast of Louisiana, clearing a major regulatory hurdle for a facility designed to load some of the world’s largest oil tankers directly in the Gulf of Mexico. U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced Thursday that the Maritime Administration (MARAD) has approved the deepwater port license application for Blue Marlin Offshore Port, a project capable of exporting up to 2 million barrels of crude oil per day. The facility will be located approximately 99 miles off Cameron Parish, Louisiana, in West Cameron Block 509. The project, developed by an affiliate of Energy Transfer, will use existing and converted offshore platform infrastructure connected to crude oil supply hubs in Texas and southwest Louisiana. Blue Marlin is designed to accommodate Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs), allowing the massive tankers to load crude directly in deep water rather than relying on more congested inland port facilities. The system will have a maximum loading rate of 80,000 barrels per hour. According to the Department of Transportation, the project is expected to support up to 1,052 construction jobs. “Building this port will unleash domestic production, create more than 1,000 good-paying construction jobs along the Gulf of America, and open vital supply lines to global markets,” Duffy said. The approval is the fourth deepwater port project cleared under the Trump administration, following the Texas GulfLink crude oil export project, Delfin LNG off Louisiana, and the $8.2 billion ST LNG project approved off Texas last week. Blue Marlin is also the second crude oil export project approved since President Trump issued his Unleashing American Energy executive order in January 2025. The decision comes as the administration moves to accelerate approvals for major offshore energy infrastructure projects. Just last week, MARAD announced approval of an $8.2 billion deepwater LNG export project off the Texas coast, saying changes to its licensing process had shortened the review timeline. Unlike that project, Blue Marlin has been working through the federal approval process for years. Its initial application was submitted in October 2020, and MARAD and the U.S. Coast Guard completed the project’s final environmental impact statement earlier this year. The offshore terminal will be supplied through a dedicated pipeline network connecting the Nederland Terminal area in Texas and other inland crude oil hubs to the offshore loading facility. The project is intended to expand U.S. crude export capacity while reducing the need for large tankers to navigate congested coastal waterways. By moving loading operations farther offshore, MARAD says the facility could also reduce vessel collision risks. The decision follows a review involving the Coast Guard, other federal agencies, and the states of Texas and Louisiana. Photo: Kate Ciembronowicz/Orsted Danish offshore wind developer Ørsted has completed its 704-megawatt Revolution Wind project off the U.S. East Coast, marking a major milestone for a development that faced repeated shutdown orders from the Trump administration. The company announced Thursday that Revolution Wind reached commercial operations in October under its power purchase agreements with utilities in Rhode Island and Connecticut, following the installation of its final wind turbines in September. The project, a joint venture between Ørsted and Skyborn Renewables, consists of 65 offshore wind turbines capable of supplying enough electricity to power more than 350,000 homes in New England. Its completion represents a significant turnaround for a project that spent much of the past year fighting to stay under construction. The Trump administration first ordered work stopped in August 2025, citing national security concerns. A federal judge subsequently allowed construction to resume, but the administration issued another suspension order in December as part of a broader effort to halt five offshore wind projects under construction along the East Coast. As gCaptain reported in January , Ørsted challenged the second suspension in federal court, arguing that the project had already invested or committed billions of dollars after undergoing extensive federal permitting and review. At the time, Revolution Wind was approximately 87% complete. A federal judge later granted a preliminary injunction allowing work to proceed. The project began producing electricity earlier this year and installed its final turbine in September before reaching full commercial operations the following month. The milestone does not necessarily end the project’s regulatory challenges. The Interior Department sought court permission in October to reconsider its earlier approval of the wind farm’s construction and operations plan, raising further questions about the administration’s approach to already-operating offshore wind projects. For Ørsted, however, Revolution Wind’s completion comes as the company reports improving operating performance across its global portfolio. In its third-quarter earnings announcement , Ørsted said earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA), excluding new partnerships and cancellation fees, rose 19% to DKK 20.2 billion ($3.0 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, compared with DKK 17.0 billion a year earlier. Third-quarter EBITDA on the same basis climbed 72% to DKK 5.26 billion, helped by stronger wind conditions, higher electricity prices and increased generation from newly completed offshore wind farms. The company nevertheless recorded a third-quarter net loss of DKK 728 million, while profit for the first nine months fell to DKK 2.6 billion from DKK 6.5 billion. Ørsted attributed the decline largely to non-cash impairments associated with rising interest rates affecting its U.S. projects. “We continue to deliver on our strategic priorities, which is translating into consistent strong financial performance,” said CEO Rasmus Errboe. The company also reported progress at its other major U.S. offshore wind development, Sunrise Wind, where installation of all wind turbine foundations has been completed. The 924-megawatt project off New York remains under construction. Elsewhere, Ørsted said Germany’s Borkum Riffgrund 3 offshore wind farm had also reached commercial operations, while construction continued at projects in Taiwan, Poland and the United Kingdom. Ørsted maintained its full-year EBITDA guidance of more than DKK 28 billion, excluding new partnerships and cancellation fees, and lowered its expected gross investments for 2026 to DKK 45 billion to DKK 50 billion. The company said the reduction reflects changes in payment timing rather than lower overall project costs. The completion of Revolution Wind is particularly notable given the uncertainty surrounding the U.S. offshore wind industry. While the Trump administration has moved aggressively to restrict new development, projects already under construction have continued advancing through legal challenges and regulatory disputes. For Revolution Wind, those battles have now given way to commercial electricity production, even as questions remain about the future of offshore wind development in the United States. articles.body: General Dynamics Mission Systems Awarded $15m MEDUSA Contract Modification Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 5, 2026 © General Dynamics Mission Systems General Dynamics Mission Systems announced it was awarded a $15 million contract modification to exercise options under a previously awarded contract for the Mining Expendable Delivery Unmanned Submarine Asset (MEDUSA). Building on the prototype, software and engineering work advanced under the July contract modification, this follow-on award continues MEDUSA's maturation and expands the program’s support infrastructure. MEDUSA is a submarine-launched delivery system that uses an expendable unmanned underwater vehicle (UUV) to deploy diverse payloads with precision. Purpose-built to meet the U.S. Navy's requirements for long-range offensive mining capability, the system offers flexibility to host additional payloads across a range of maritime missions. Work began in September 2026 and will continue through February 2028 at General Dynamics facilities in Quincy and Taunton, Massachusetts. The Naval Sea Systems Command, Washington Navy Yard, District of Columbia, is the contracting activity. General Dynamics has invested in its facilities and staff to support the growth of its UUV centers of excellence and advance undersea programs. These include the Center of Excellence for Research and Development, Prototyping, and Offshore Test in Quincy and the UUV Manufacturing and Assembly Center of Excellence in Taunton. Together, these sites provide an integrated path from concept through production. The Quincy facility supports rapid prototyping and in-water testing, while the Taunton facility provides the advanced manufacturing capacity to transition mature designs toward full-rate production. Alongside these investments, General Dynamics is working with suppliers to strengthen the industrial base and expand production capacity to meet the U.S. Navy’s future demands.

articles.summary: Twin Disc, Inc. subsidiary Katsa announced that it is expanding its capacity with a 54,000-square-foot gearbox assembly facility and warehouse in Pirkkala, Finland, in response to a double-digit percentage year-over-year increase in demand.The new plant…
articles.body: Katsa Expands Capacity With New Assembly Plant Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 5, 2026 Overhead view of Katsa's new 54,000-square-foot gearbox assembly facility and warehouse that's currently under construction in Pirkkala, Finland. © Katsa Twin Disc, Inc. subsidiary Katsa announced that it is expanding its capacity with a 54,000-square-foot gearbox assembly facility and warehouse in Pirkkala, Finland, in response to a double-digit percentage year-over-year increase in demand. The new plant, expected to be fully operational by May 2027, brings together gearbox assembly, testing and painting under one roof. The unified design will streamline operations by reducing material handling steps and maximizing production flow. In addition, a dedicated warehouse will support efficient inbound and outbound logistics for components from suppliers and from Katsa’s nearby Tampere manufacturing plant and provide on-site storage. Katsas growth is driven by demand from multiple industries, including defense, industrial power generation and heavy equipment. While Katsa does not supply gearboxes directly to data centers, it provides components to major engine manufacturers who design and install backup power systems for these facilities. The company is currently adding 40 employees at its manufacturing operations and its two existing assembly locations in Tampere and will transition 25 experienced workers to the new facility in Pirkkala. By June 2027, Katsa expects to have a total workforce of approximately 250 employees. The site will feature a new 20-ton overhead crane-doubling the lifting capacity of Katsa's current assembly operation-and will enable the company to assemble and test larger industrial gearboxes. The facility will also include a renewable energy heating and cooling system. Ten geothermal wells, each about 1,150 feet deep, will provide approximately 98% of the building's heating and cooling needs. Construction recently reached a major milestone with the completion of the building's roof. To celebrate, Katsa hosted a traditional Finnish harjakaiset (topping off) ceremony.

articles.summary: Maritime experts warn that the westward spread of attacks between Russia and Ukraine, toward NATO coastlines, is now having commercial consequences.
